1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6.strategy: Opens the diagonal for the king's bishop and keeps Black's set-up flexible: Black can pin a knight, fianchetto the queen's bishop or challenge the centre at once, and chooses only after seeing White's third move. The price is the c8-bishop, which the e6-pawn shuts in, so it usually comes out via a fianchetto.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop and castle, and lets White build a broad pawn centre that Black then attacks from the flank. The positions are sharp and unbalanced, usually with play on opposite wings, and both sides play for a win. The price is White's extra space and a large body of theory.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5.strategy: Hits d4 at once and aims for a queenside pawn majority, backed by a fianchettoed king's bishop. Black gives White space and a strong pawn on d5 in return, so Black must find active play before the cramp tells. The games are unbalanced and often sharp.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6.name: Old Indian Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6.background: Siegbert Tarrasch introduced it in 1902, but it is more commonly associated with Mikhail Chigorin, who adopted it five years later and pioneered it late in his career. It has never attained the popularity of the King's Indian, though some King's Indian players use it to avoid the Sämisch and Averbakh Variations.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6.strategy: Prepares ...e5 with a compact set-up and keeps the choice between a solid bishop on e7 and a King's Indian fianchetto open. It is solid but usually cramped, because the bishop on e7 is less active than one on g7, and it lacks the dynamic chances of the King's Indian.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Nc6.name: Black Knights' Tango
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Nc6.background: It originated in the 1920s with the Mexican grandmaster Carlos Torre, hence the name Mexican Defence, and the American master Alexander Kevitz. After decades of obscurity, the International Master Georgi Orlov revived it with a booklet in 1992 and a book in 1998 and renamed it the Black Knights' Tango.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and presses on d4 so that ...e5 can follow, hoping to induce White to push its pawns too early. The knight blocks the c-pawn, and a developing reply discourages ...e5, so Black often switches to a more modest set-up. Sound but offbeat, and highly transpositional.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c6.name: Slav Indian
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 and a solid pawn chain, with the c8-bishop still free to come out before the e-pawn shuts it in. The c-pawn is committed early, so a quick ...c5 would cost a tempo, but Black can still build a compact pawn centre instead.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 b6.name: Accelerated Queen's Indian Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 b6.background: It is considered less accurate than the standard Queen's Indian move order 2...e6 3.Nf3 b6: in Alekhine–König, Vienna 1922, White was better after 3.Nc3 Bb7 4.Qc2 d5 5.cxd5 Nxd5 6.Nf3. James Plaskett and Raymond Keene analyse the line in their 1987 book on the English Defence.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 to control e4 and d5. Until the e-pawn moves, the f8-bishop cannot pin a knight on c3, so White can develop and prepare e4 freely; stopping that with ...d5 lets White gain time against the knight after the exchange on d5.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5.name: Budapest Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5.background: The first known game was a casual game between Mór Adler and Géza Maróczy in Budapest on 5 March 1896. It gained attention when Milan Vidmar beat Akiba Rubinstein with it at Berlin in April 1918, the year Carl Schlechter published a monograph that can be considered the first book on the opening.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5.strategy: Sacrifices a pawn for quick development and active piece play, and usually wins it back. White can try to keep the extra pawn or return it for a lead in development, so the game turns on whether Black's activity outweighs the material. Rarely played at grandmaster level.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d5.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Marshall Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d5.background: Frank Marshall played it in the 1920s but gave it up after losing with it to Alexander Alekhine at Baden-Baden in 1925. It is regarded as a fairly dubious variation of the Queen's Gambit Declined, and experienced players no longer use it.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d5.strategy: Claims the centre at once, but White simply takes it: after 3.cxd5 Nxd5 4.Nf3, White gains time against the knight and builds a broad centre without allowing the counter ...e5.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 b5.name: Indian Defence: Pyrenees Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 b5.strategy: Offers a pawn for queenside pressure, but without a pawn on d5 and without ...c5 to open the queenside. After 3.cxb5 White is a clean pawn ahead, and the pressure along the queenside does not make up for it while White develops in peace.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 a6.strategy: Prepares ...b5 and keeps White's pieces off b5, but does nothing for the centre or development. Black spends a tempo on a rook-pawn move while White builds the centre at leisure.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 a5.strategy: Stops b4 but contributes nothing to development or the fight for the centre. A tempo is spent on the rook's pawn while White occupies the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Na6.strategy: Develops the knight to the rim, where it eyes b4 and c5 and can recapture on c5 if Black strikes there with the c-pawn. From a6 it does nothing for d5 or e5, and White takes an easy central edge.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 h6.strategy: Prevents Bg5 but spends a tempo on a rook-pawn move and leaves the centre alone. White simply builds the centre and has a lead in development.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 h5.strategy: Spends a tempo on the rook's pawn and does nothing for the centre or development; with the pawn past h6, Black can no longer meet Bg5 with ...h6. White develops freely, builds the centre and has a clear lead in development.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Ng8.strategy: Undoes the knight's development and costs two tempi. White has a full centre and the move, and Black has to start again with ...Nf6.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Ng4.strategy: Moves the same knight a second time without a target: f2 and h2 are both guarded, and h3 can drive it back later. White builds the centre and gains further time against the knight.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Nh5.strategy: Moves the knight a second time, to the rim, where its only forward squares, f4 and g3, are covered by White. White takes the centre and is clearly ahead in development.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Ne4.strategy: Moves the knight again to e4, where Qc2 or f3 chase it with a gain of time. Black has no pawn on d5 or f5 yet to support it, and White builds a broad centre with the time gained.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Rg8.strategy: Wastes a tempo with the rook and forfeits the right to castle kingside for good, while the centre and development are untouched.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g5.name: Indian Defence: Medusa Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g5.strategy: Loses a pawn at once: 3.Bxg5 wins it, and after 3...Ne4 the bishop simply retreats while the weakened kingside leaves Black no real compensation.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Nd5.strategy: Hangs the knight: 3.cxd5 wins it for nothing, because the d7-pawn blocks the queen's defence of d5 and no other piece guards the square.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d5 3.cxd5.strategy: Settles the tension in White's favour: Black has no c- or e-pawn ready to recapture, so a piece has to retake and can be driven away by a big pawn centre. White gets space and the initiative against a dubious early ...d5.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d5 3.Nc3.strategy: Ignores the provocation and develops: the game drops into familiar queen's-pawn structures in which Black's early knight move is no handicap. White keeps a comfortable lead in space and a flexible centre, but passes up the chance to punish the odd move order.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d5 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops and guards the centre, inviting ...dxc4, after which the check on a4 wins the pawn straight back. White gets a sound, ordinary game, without the lasting initiative that the exchange on d5 brings.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d5 3.cxd5 c6.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Marshall Defence, Tan Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d5 3.cxd5 c6.strategy: Gambits a pawn for quick development and open lines: after the exchange on c6 Black aims for a central break and an early queen trade. White keeps the extra pawn and a small edge in the queenless middlegame, so Black must play for activity.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d5 3.cxd5 Nxd5.strategy: The natural recapture: the knight takes the pawn back from a developed square, so Black is not a pawn down. On d5 it can be hit with tempo, and White gets space and the initiative, so Black must look for counterplay against a larger centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d5 3.cxd5 Qxd5.strategy: Brings the queen out early, and Nc3 hits it at once, so White develops with tempo while the queen looks for a square. Grabbing the b2 pawn later walks into Rb1 and Nb5 and loses.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d5 3.cxd5 g6.strategy: Hopes White develops naturally so that the pawn can be retaken later, but White can simply check on a4: the pawn on d5 is then hard to win back and Black has little to show for it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3.strategy: The principal move: it develops a piece towards the centre and prepares e4. White wants a classical pawn centre, and Black has to contest it with pieces and well-timed pawn breaks, since waiting would leave White with much more space.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the kingside knight and covers e5, keeping the choice of set-up open. It claims less space at once than a knight on c3 and leaves Black free to fianchetto the king's bishop or develop it modestly.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.g4.name: Old Indian Defence: Aged Gibbon Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.g4.strategy: Offers a pawn with nothing developed to defend it: Black simply takes it with the knight or the bishop. White has loosened the kingside and has little to show for the pawn.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 e5.name: Old Indian Defence: Ukrainian Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 e5.strategy: Occupies the centre with a pawn backed by d6 and challenges White's plan of building a big pawn centre. Black accepts a compact structure with a little less space, but a solid one in which every piece has a clear job.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Bf5.name: Old Indian Defence: Janowski Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Bf5.background: Dawid Janowski introduced 3...Bf5 in the 1920s, but it gained little popularity until the 1980s. Mikhail Tal, Bent Larsen, Florin Gheorghiu and Kamran Shirazi have each played it several times.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Bf5.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain before it can be shut in, and stops White's space grab: 4.e4 would simply lose a pawn to ...Nxe4. The price is that the bishop on f5 needs care later, and Black still has to settle the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Nbd7.strategy: Develops the knight to support ...e5 and keeps the c-pawn free. It is a flexible, solid choice, but White can take the full centre at once, so Black accepts being a little cramped.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 c6.name: Old Indian Defence: Czech Variation, with Nc3
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 c6.strategy: A solid, flexible move: the c6 pawn takes d5 and b5 from White's pieces and keeps ...e5 in reserve. It takes the natural square c6 from the queen's knight and leaves White the first say in the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Bf5 4.f3.name: Old Indian Defence: Janowski Variation, Main Line
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Bf5 4.f3.strategy: Prepares e4 with the support of a pawn, so that the knight and bishop can no longer win it. White still builds the broad centre it wants, at the cost of loosening the e1-h4 diagonal and taking the natural square from the g1 knight.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Bf5 4.g3.name: Old Indian Defence: Janowski Variation, Fianchetto Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Bf5 4.g3.strategy: A quiet answer to the bishop's idea: the fianchettoed bishop on g2 will guard e4, so White can still prepare a central advance. A low-risk choice that claims less space than a big pawn centre but keeps long-term pressure on the long diagonal.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Bf5 4.e4.name: Old Indian Defence: Janowski Variation, Grinberg Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Bf5 4.e4.strategy: Offers the e-pawn at once. Black takes it with the knight, and after the knights are exchanged the bishop takes again, because e4 has two attackers and only one defender. White gets little for the pawn.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nf3.name: Old Indian Defence: Two Knights Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nf3.strategy: The principal move: it develops with an attack on e5, which Black has to support at once, and keeps the choice between holding the tension and exchanging on e5. White keeps a healthy lead in space without committing the pawns.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 e5 4.e3.strategy: Supports d4 with a pawn and frees the bishop instead of facing the tension on e5. It is solid but passive: Black gets time to finish development and White gives up the chance of an active centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 e5 4.dxe5.strategy: Releases the tension and offers to trade queens after ...dxe5, which forces Black's king to move. Black's king is safe enough, the pieces coordinate well and the bishop is freed, so White gains no lasting edge.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 e5 4.e3 Nbd7.strategy: Defends e5 with a developing move and keeps the structure healthy. Against the quiet set-up Black needs nothing special: development and a firm hold on the centre are enough for an easy game.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 e5 4.e3 Be7.strategy: Develops the bishop modestly and prepares castling, keeping e5 protected and the structure solid. The bishop is less active than on a fianchetto, but Black has no weaknesses and a safe king.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 e5 4.e3 exd4.strategy: Trades the e-pawn for White's d-pawn at once and opens the e-file. Black's pieces come out easily, but White recaptures with the e-pawn, keeping a compact centre and more space, so Black has conceded the centre for activity.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 e5 4.e3 Nbd7 5.Bd.name: Old Indian Defence: Duz-Khotimirsky Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 e5 4.e3 Nbd7 5.Bd.strategy: Develops the bishop on its active diagonal, where it supports a later e4 advance. White accepts a slow, solid build-up in which Black can complete development safely, and the fight for the centre is put off.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 e5 4.e3 Nbd7 5.Nf.strategy: Develops with pressure on e5, which is attacked twice and defended twice. White keeps the tension and can release it later, with a safe king after castling and a small but lasting lead in space.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 e5 4.e3 Nbd7 5.Be.strategy: Puts the bishop on a safe square and prepares castling, leaving the knight to decide the set-up later. It is flexible and undemanding, but it asks little of Black, who completes development without difficulty.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Nbd7 4.e4.strategy: Takes the full centre at once. With the knight already on d7, Black has no quick way to hit the e-pawn, and White's space advantage will last. Black has to counter with piece play and a well-timed pawn lever.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Nbd7 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops first and keeps the choice of centre for later: if Black plays ...e5, White takes the centre with e4 and the game reaches the main line anyway. It leaves Black a little more freedom, for instance to fianchetto the king's bishop.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Nbd7 4.g3.strategy: Prepares a fianchetto of the king's bishop and a quieter game. White gives up the chance to build a big pawn centre at once, and Black, free to occupy the middle with ...e5, equalises without much trouble.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Nbd7 4.e4 e5.strategy: Challenges the big centre immediately. The pawn is backed by d6 and by the knight, so Black keeps a compact and well-protected structure, accepting a little less space for a solid position without weaknesses.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Nbd7 4.e4 g6.strategy: Fianchettoes the king's bishop and lets White keep the big centre for now, planning to undermine it later from the flank with the bishop on the long diagonal. Black trades some space for a flexible position with counterplay.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Nbd7 4.e4 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 from the flank instead of contesting e4 directly. White can close the centre and keep the space edge, or open it and trade a central pawn; either way Black plays on the queenside with less room.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Nbd7 4.e4 e5 5.Nf.name: Old Indian Defence: Normal Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Nbd7 4.e4 e5 5.Nf.strategy: Develops with an attack on e5, which is attacked twice and defended twice. White keeps its pawns on d4 and e4 together and can choose later whether to release the tension or hold it, with more space in either case.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Nbd7 4.e4 e5 5.Be.strategy: Keeps everything protected and prepares castling, leaving White free to choose between holding the tension and releasing it. It puts less pressure on e5 than a knight move, so Black develops without difficulty.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Nbd7 4.e4 e5 5.d5.strategy: Closes the centre and takes space. Black's knight gets a good square on c5 with an attack on e4, so White must keep defending the e-pawn; the pawn structure is fixed and both sides play on the wings.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Nbd7 4.e4 e5 5.Nf.strategy: Chooses to fianchetto the king's bishop rather than develop it modestly. Black aims for a compact structure with castling and a bishop behind the firm e5 pawn, and accepts a closed centre in which White keeps more space.

Develops the bishop modestly and prepares castling, keeping e5 fully protected. Black accepts a smaller share of the centre in return for a compact position without weaknesses; White keeps a small edge.
Takes d5 from White's pieces and keeps the centre firm, but spends a tempo while the king's bishop is still at home. Black stays solid, and White's lead in space remains.

Brings the bishop to a safe square and prepares castling without weakening the centre. White's modest development keeps the d4 and e4 pawns protected and the space advantage intact, and leaves the question of the e5 tension open.
Pins the f6 knight against the queen to add pressure to the centre. Black asks the bishop at once with ...h6, so White has spent time and given the bishop a target without a lasting gain.

Develops toward the kingside and adds a defender to e4. The bishop can be harassed by a knight coming to c5, so White may lose a tempo, and the move gives the centre no more than a safer square would.

Completes the fianchetto and prepares castling. The bishop stands behind its own e5 pawn, so it works more as a defender than as an attacker for now. Black's position is solid and short of space, and the bishop becomes active only if the centre opens.

Trades the e-pawn for White's d-pawn, putting a white knight on d4 in the centre. Black's pieces become freer and the bishop later gets a clear diagonal, but White keeps the extra space and a stable centre.
Takes d5 away from White and keeps the centre closed and solid. It spends a tempo while the king's bishop is undeveloped, so Black stays cramped rather than active.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nf3 Bg4.name: Old Indian Defence: Tartakower-Indian
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nf3 Bg4.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain and attacks the knight on f3, which guards d4 and e5. Black can trade it off, and a pawn recapture would double White's pawns, so Black develops with a small threat and keeps the centre contested.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nf3 c6.name: Old Indian Defence: Czech Variation, with Nf3
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nf3 c6.strategy: Prepares a solid centre with a pawn on c6 that takes d5 and b5 from White's pieces. It takes the natural square from the queen's knight and does not challenge White's centre, so Black waits to see what White does.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nf3 g6.strategy: Fianchettoes the king's bishop and lets White occupy the centre first, planning to attack it later from the flank. Black accepts less space for a flexible, compact position with counterplay on the long diagonal.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nf3 Nbd7.strategy: Develops the queen's knight and prepares to challenge the centre with the e-pawn. A compact, solid set-up, but Black gives White the choice of how to build the centre, and the bishop's route is not yet decided.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5.name: Indian Defence: Budapest Gambit Accepted
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5.strategy: Accepts the gambit and gains a tempo, since the pawn on e5 attacks the knight. White is a pawn up with the sounder structure, but Black has quick development and play against e5 in return, so the question is how long White can hold the pawn and what it costs.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.e3.strategy: Declines the gambit by letting Black take on d4 and recapturing with a pawn, which keeps a healthy centre and avoids the sharp play. It is sound but gives White no edge: Black develops freely with a check on b4 and castles with an easy game.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.Nf3.strategy: Defends the d4 pawn and develops, but Black pushes the e-pawn at once, attacking the knight and gaining space and a tempo. The knight must go to a less comfortable square, so White has handed Black the initiative in the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4.name: Indian Defence: Budapest Gambit Accepted, Main Line
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4.strategy: The main line: the knight leaves the attacked square for one from which it hits e5 at once, so the pawn is only borrowed. White must choose between giving it back for development and space, or defending it at a structural price, while Black plays for quick development and active piece play.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ne4.name: Indian Defence: Budapest Gambit Accepted, Fajarowicz Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ne4.background: Said to have its origins in the chess circles of Leipzig, the first important game being H. Steiner against Fajarowicz at the 1928 Wiesbaden tournament.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ne4.strategy: Leaves the pawn alone and puts the knight on a central square where it eyes f2 and c3, playing for piece activity and tactical tricks instead of material. If White defuses the tricks, Black has simply given a pawn without lasting compensation.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Nc6.strategy: Ignores the attack on the knight in order to hit e5: White simply takes the knight with the pawn, and recapturing on f6 wins back only a pawn. Black is a whole piece down with nothing to show for it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Nh5.strategy: Saves the knight, but only to the rim, where it attacks nothing and does not help to win back e5. Black has given a pawn without gaining development or a tempo, and White can consolidate the extra pawn at leisure.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ne4 4.a3.name: Indian Defence: Budapest Gambit Accepted, Fajarowicz Defence, Bonsdorf Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ne4 4.a3.strategy: Takes the b4 square from Black's bishop and from a knight arriving on c6, which removes the checks and jumps that would harass White, and prepares to attack the knight with the queen. The critical test of the line: Black has few ways to justify the lost pawn.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ne4 4.Qc2.name: Indian Defence: Budapest Gambit Accepted, Fajarowicz Defence, Steiner Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ne4 4.Qc2.strategy: Attacks the knight at once, so a retreat would give up Black's lead in development, the only compensation for the pawn. Black must keep the knight in place by developing with check and supporting it with a pawn, which is by no means easy but leaves real counterplay.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ne4 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops a piece while defending the extra pawn and covering the d2 square, so that the check on b4 can be met by a knight move that keeps White's pawns intact. A calm way to hold the material, leaving Black to prove the pawn was worth it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Bf4.name: Indian Defence: Budapest Gambit Accepted, Main Line, Rubinstein Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Bf4.background: Named after the game Rubinstein against Vidmar at Berlin in 1918, in which 4.Bf4 was first played. Various authors consider it the most dangerous move for Black.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Bf4.strategy: The main line: the bishop guards e5 and stays outside the pawn chain, so a Black bishop on c5 can be met by e3, which opens the queen against the knight. White then chooses between keeping the pawn at the price of doubled pawns, or returning it for a sound structure and the bishop pair.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Nf3.name: Indian Defence: Budapest Gambit Accepted, Main Line, Adler Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Nf3.background: Named after the game between Adler and Maróczy in Budapest in 1896.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops and defends e5, yet White is ready to give the pawn back: a Black bishop on c5 hits f2 and forces a pawn move that shuts in White's own bishop, so e5 has too few defenders. White plays for quick development, d5 and the long diagonal; Black regains the pawn and swings a rook towards White's king.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.e4.name: Indian Defence: Budapest Gambit Accepted, Main Line, Alekhine Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.e4.background: Named after Alekhine for his wins with it against Rabinovich at Baden-Baden in 1925 and Seitz at Hastings. Its reputation stayed mixed, as he lost with it to Gilg at Semmering the same year.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.e4.strategy: Gives the pawn back at once, but with tempo: the queen now eyes the knight on g4. In return White gets a broad pawn centre, a grip on d5 and extra space, and has to play precisely, since the centre becomes the target of Black's counterplay.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.e4 Nxe5.name: Indian Defence: Budapest Gambit Accepted, Main Line, Alekhine Variation, Abonyi Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.e4 Nxe5.strategy: Regains the pawn at once with a knight that lands in the centre, where it hits c4. A pawn push will soon ask it to move again, so Black must choose its next square with care; if that goes well, Black has a solid structure and active pieces against White's space.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.e4 d6.name: Indian Defence: Budapest Gambit Accepted, Main Line, Alekhine Variation, Tartakower Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.e4 d6.strategy: Tries to keep the gambit alive by developing at the pawn's expense, but the compensation falls short: White takes on d6 and a bishop move hits the knight on g4 with tempo, leaving White a pawn ahead with the better game.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.e4 h5.strategy: Keeps the knight on g4, supported by the h-pawn, and leaves the e5 pawn alone to play for development. It is only a weakness: after Be2 Black cannot take on e5 without losing the h5 pawn to the bishop, so the knight is driven back and White keeps the better game.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Nc6 3.d5.strategy: Gains space with tempo by attacking the c6 knight and fixing the centre. It is ambitious but commits the pawns early, and the knight finds a good square at once, so White's gain is space rather than development.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nf3.strategy: The most common reply: the knight develops and covers e5, so Black's ...e5 break is no longer free and the knight on c6 loses much of its point. White keeps a flexible, solid centre and Black has to settle for a slower set-up.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight and puts pressure on d5 and e4. It allows Black's central break, which White meets by gaining space and driving the c6 knight back, so the game turns sharp and unbalanced rather than giving White a clear edge.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Nc6 3.d5 Ne5.strategy: The natural answer: the knight steps to a strong central square from which it attacks the undefended c4 pawn. White has to deal with that before anything else, so Black has used the tempo well.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Nc6 3.d5 Nb8.strategy: Retreats the attacked knight to its starting square. It is solid, and White's advanced pawns give Black targets to work against, but Black has spent two moves on this knight while White has gained space, so the cost is time.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Nc6 3.d5 Nb4.strategy: Steps aside to a square that eyes d5 and c2, both guarded. After a3 the knight must go to a6, from where it can head for c5, so the move is playable, but Black loses time and White gains space.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Nc6 3.d5 Ne5 4.f4.name: Black Knights' Tango: Horsefly Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Nc6 3.d5 Ne5 4.f4.strategy: A gambit: the f-pawn attacks the knight but leaves c4 undefended, so Black simply takes it with the knight. White hopes for activity and the initiative in return, but loosens the kingside and is a pawn down with no clear compensation.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Nc6 3.d5 Ne5 4.e4.strategy: Answers the attack on c4 by opening the bishop's diagonal, so ...Nxc4 loses a piece, and builds a broad pawn centre at the same time. Taking on e4 fails too: the queen forks the two knights. Black has to undermine the centre, and the game is sharp and balanced.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Nc6 3.d5 Ne5 4.Nd2.strategy: Defends c4 with a piece and keeps the pawn. It is safe, but the knight blocks the c1-bishop and the queen and has little scope there, so Black gets time to attack the advanced centre.
